section.title: The Covenant Renewed
section.sectionRationale: God answers Moses' plea by proclaiming His own name in the fullest revelation of His character in the Old Testament, then renews the covenant broken by the golden calf. Moses returns with his face radiant from being in God's presence, so bright he must wear a veil before the people.
section.thesis: God proclaims His name as compassionate, gracious, and just, renews His covenant with Israel after the golden calf, and Moses descends with a face so radiant from being in God's presence that he must veil it before the people.
section.frameNote: Four movements: new tablets and God's proclamation of His own name and character; the terms of the renewed covenant; the command to write these words after forty days on the mountain; and Moses' radiant, veiled face.

units.label: The LORD proclaims His name
units.note: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger

media.alt: A figure bowed low before a cloud on a mountain
media.caption: The LORD passes before Moses and proclaims His own name and character.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, and I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.
Be ready in the morning, and come up on Mount Sinai to present yourself before Me on the mountaintop.
No one may go up with you; in fact, no one may be seen anywhere on the mountain, not even the flocks or herds may graze in front of the mountain.”
So Moses chiseled out two stone tablets like the originals. He rose early in the morning, and taking the two stone tablets in his hands, he went up Mount Sinai as the LORD had commanded him.
And the LORD descended in a cloud, stood with him there, and proclaimed His name, the LORD.
Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: “The LORD, the LORD God, is {{compassionate|compassionate and gracious}}, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,

maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generations.”
Moses immediately bowed down to the ground and worshiped.
“O Lord,” he said, “if I have indeed found favor in Your sight, my Lord, please go with us. Although this is a stiff-necked people, forgive our iniquity and sin, and take us as Your inheritance.”

units.label: The terms of the renewed covenant
units.note: make no treaty with the inhabitants of the land

verses.text: And the LORD said, “Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will perform wonders that have never been done in any nation in all the world. All the people among whom you live will see the LORD's work, for it is an awesome thing that I am doing with you.
Observe what I command you this day. I will drive out before you the Amorites, Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
Be careful not to make a treaty with the inhabitants of the land you are entering, lest they become a snare in your midst.
Rather, you must tear down their altars, smash their sacred stones, and chop down their Asherah poles.
For you must not worship any other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.
Do not make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, for when they prostitute themselves to their gods and sacrifice to them, they will invite you, and you will eat their sacrifices.
And when you take some of their daughters as brides for your sons, their daughters will prostitute themselves to their gods and cause your sons to do the same.
You shall make no molten gods for yourselves.

You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, you are to eat unleavened bread as I commanded you. For in the month of Abib you came out of Egypt.
The first offspring of every womb belongs to Me, including all the firstborn males among your livestock, whether cattle or sheep.

You must redeem the firstborn of a donkey with a lamb; but if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. You must redeem all the firstborn of your sons. No one shall appear before Me empty-handed.
Six days you shall labor, but on the seventh day you shall rest; even in the seasons of plowing and harvesting, you must rest.
And you are to celebrate the Feast of Weeks with the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering at the turn of the year.
Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel.
For I will drive out the nations before you and enlarge your borders, and no one will covet your land when you go up three times a year to appear before the LORD your God.
Do not offer the blood of a sacrifice to Me along with anything leavened, and do not let any of the sacrifice from the Passover Feast remain until morning.
Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother's milk.”
The LORD also said to Moses, “Write down these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.”
So Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights without eating bread or drinking water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.

units.label: The radiant, veiled face
units.note: he was unaware his face had become radiant

media.alt: A veiled face descending a mountain
media.caption: Moses veils his radiant face after speaking with the LORD.

verses.text: And when Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the Testimony in his hands, he was unaware that his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD.
Aaron and all the Israelites looked at Moses, and behold, his face was radiant. And they were afraid to approach him.
But Moses called out to them; so Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses spoke to them.
And after this all the Israelites came near, and Moses commanded them to do everything that the LORD had told him on Mount Sinai.
When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a {{veil|veil}} over his face.
But whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with Him, he would remove the veil until he came out. And when he came out, he would tell the Israelites what he had been commanded,
and the Israelites would see that the face of Moses was radiant. So Moses would put the veil back over his face until he went in to speak with the LORD.

compassionate.gloss: Compassionate and gracious, the opening words of the fullest self-revelation of God's character in the Old Testament. This proclamation becomes the most quoted description of God's nature throughout the rest of Scripture, especially in the Psalms and Prophets.

veil.gloss: A veil, covering Moses' radiant face after he had spoken with the LORD. Paul later contrasts this veil, which faded and had to be reapplied, with the unveiled, ever increasing glory believers now behold in Christ, 2 Corinthians 3:13-18.

basic.context: God tells Moses to chisel new tablets and returns to the mountain, where He passes before him and proclaims His own name and character in the fullest terms found anywhere in the Old Testament: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, yet also just. God then renews the covenant with specific terms for life in the land, and Moses comes down with a face so radiant he must wear a veil before the people.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, historical renewal of the covenant after Israel's idolatry, not a repeatable ritual. God's proclaimed name in verses 6 and 7 functions as a genuine, foundational self-revelation that shapes the rest of the Bible's understanding of who God is, holding together mercy and justice without minimizing either.
basic.originalLanguages: God proclaims Himself rachum ve-chanun, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, yet the same proclamation insists He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. Moses' face becomes radiant from being in God's presence, requiring a masveh, veil, whenever he was not actively speaking with the people on God's behalf.
basic.typology: Moses' fading radiance, requiring a veil reapplied again and again, points to the temporary and partial nature of the old covenant's glory. Paul directly contrasts this with the greater, unfading glory believers behold in Christ, whose glory is not diminished or veiled from those who trust Him.
basic.christ: Paul in 2 Corinthians 3 explicitly interprets Moses' veil as a picture of a covenant that was fading, contrasted with the new covenant in Christ, whose glory believers behold with unveiled faces, being transformed into His likeness with ever increasing glory, 2 Corinthians 3:7-18. The very name proclaimed here, compassionate, gracious, forgiving, yet just, finds its full resolution at the cross, where God's justice and mercy meet.
basic.god: This proclamation of God's name is arguably Scripture's fullest self-description of His character, holding together compassion, patience, and forgiving love with an unwavering commitment to justice. God is neither a soft sentimentalist nor a cold judge; He is both merciful and holy at once, and this tension is resolved fully only at the cross.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Corinthians 3:7-18 interprets Moses' veil as picturing the fading old covenant, contrasted with believers' unveiled access to Christ's glory. Numbers 14:18 and Psalm 103:8 both quote this proclamation of God's name directly. Nehemiah 9:17 recalls it when Israel again faces judgment for sin.
basic.oneStory: After Israel's great betrayal, God proclaims His own name as both merciful and just, renews His covenant, and Moses' face shines with a fading glory that must be veiled. This partial, fading glory anticipates the permanent, unveiled glory believers now behold in Christ, in whom God's mercy and justice meet completely and forever.

context.literary:
Exodus 34 is the answer to Exodus 32, and it is built so that the reader hears the echoes. The tablets that were broken are replaced 'like the originals,' verse 1 and verse 4. The people who made 'a molten calf,' Exodus 32:4, are told 'You shall make no molten gods for yourselves,' verse 17. The false 'feast to the LORD' of Exodus 32:5 is replaced by the true feasts of verses 18 to 23. Aaron, who once fashioned the calf, is now among those afraid to come near Moses, verse 30.

The chapter opens by recalling the first ascent. As in Exodus 19:12-13, no one else may go up, not even the flocks may graze near the mountain, verse 3. Moses rises early with the tablets in his hands, verse 4, and he will come down with them in his hands, verse 29, an inclusio that frames the whole renewal.

At the centre stands the proclamation of verses 6 and 7, the fulfilment of the promise made in Exodus 33:19-22. The LORD descends in the cloud, stands with Moses, passes by, and calls out His name. The speech has a deliberate imbalance. Five phrases describe mercy and fidelity before a single clause of judgment, and mercy extends 'to a thousand generations' while iniquity is visited 'to the third and fourth.'

Moses' response in verses 8 and 9 gathers up the vocabulary of the two previous chapters: 'found favor,' 'go with us,' 'stiff-necked,' 'forgive.' The covenant terms that follow in verses 10 to 26 closely parallel Exodus 23:12-19 and the opening of the Ten Commandments, but the selection is pointed. Almost every clause concerns exclusive worship: no treaties, no foreign altars, no other god, no molten gods, and a calendar of feasts that brings Israel before the LORD.

The last movement repeats two words three times each. Moses' face is 'radiant' in verses 29, 30 and 35, and he puts on or removes the 'veil' in verses 33, 34 and 35. The book is preparing for its final scene, when glory fills the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34.
context.historical:
The setting is again the summit of Sinai, and the renewal follows the second forty days Moses spent there, verse 28. Deuteronomy says he neither ate bread nor drank water during both periods, Deuteronomy 9:9 and 9:18, the second spent pleading for the people after the calf.

The covenant terms assume life in Canaan. The nations named in verse 11 are the peoples of the land, and verse 13 names three features of their worship. Altars were places of sacrifice. 'Sacred stones' were standing stones set up at shrines as markers of a deity's presence. 'Asherah poles' were wooden cult objects associated with the goddess Asherah, known from texts at Ugarit as the consort of the high god El. The BSB footnote at verse 12 notes that 'treaty' translates berit, the same word as 'covenant.' Israel may not cut a covenant with the nations because it has cut one with the LORD.

The feasts follow Israel's agricultural year. The Feast of Unleavened Bread fell in Abib, which the BSB footnote places in March and April, and recalled the exodus, verse 18. The Feast of Weeks, later called Pentecost, came with the wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering, later Tabernacles, at the turn of the year, verse 22. Three times a year every male was to appear before the LORD, leaving homes and fields undefended, and God promises that 'no one will covet your land' while they go, verse 24.

Verse 20 reflects the value of animals in the ancient economy. The donkey was not a sacrificial animal, so its firstborn was redeemed with a lamb or else killed, as in Exodus 13:12-13. The command not to cook a young goat in its mother's milk, verse 26, appears also in Exodus 23:19 and Deuteronomy 14:21. The text gives no reason. Jewish tradition built its separation of meat and milk on it; others have suggested it forbade a particular pagan rite or preserved a boundary between life and death.

The word for Moses' radiant face, qaran, is related to qeren, horn. Jerome's Latin rendered it 'horned,' which is why medieval art, and Michelangelo's statue, show Moses with horns.
context.canonical:
The name proclaimed in verses 6 and 7 becomes Israel's creed. Moses prays it back to God in Numbers 14:18 when the people refuse to enter the land. The returned exiles recite it in Nehemiah 9:17. The psalmists sing it in Psalm 86:15, 103:8 and 145:8. Joel uses it to call the people to return, 'rend your hearts and not your garments,' Joel 2:13. Jonah quotes it as a complaint, because he knew God would spare Nineveh, Jonah 4:2. Nahum quotes the other half, that the LORD 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' against Nineveh in a later generation, Nahum 1:3. Micah turns it into a question of wonder: 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?' Micah 7:18.

The covenant terms are echoed in Deuteronomy's instructions for entering the land, and Deuteronomy 10:1-5 records that the second tablets were placed in the ark, 'and there they have remained.' The warning about intermarriage with the nations shapes the later reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah.

The New Testament takes up the chapter in two main ways. John describes the incarnate Word as 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, and says that 'the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17. Many readers hear in 'grace and truth' an echo of 'loving devotion and faithfulness' in verse 6. The Feast of Weeks of verse 22 becomes the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:1, when the Spirit is given. And Paul devotes a long passage, 2 Corinthians 3:7-18, to Moses' radiant face and veil. He calls the glory of the old covenant 'fleeting,' and he contrasts the veil Moses wore with the unveiled faces of those who turn to the Lord, 2 Corinthians 3:16-18. James gathers up the character of verse 6 in a phrase: 'The Lord is full of compassion and mercy,' James 5:11.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know the God who had spared them. After the calf, the question in every Israelite's mind would have been, what kind of God is this, who threatens destruction and then renews a covenant? The answer comes not from Moses' theology but from God's own mouth. God interprets His name, and every later Israelite would hear in it the reason they still existed.

He meant them to see that God's mercy is not the absence of justice. The same proclamation that forgives 'iniquity, transgression, and sin' also refuses to clear the guilty, verse 7. Israel had just seen both. They were forgiven as a people, and yet three thousand died and a plague struck. The name explains why both are true.

He also meant them to understand that renewal comes with renewed terms. The covenant is restored on God's initiative, 'Behold, I am making a covenant,' verse 10, but it is not a covenant without demands. Almost every command of verses 11 to 26 targets the sin of the calf and the temptations of Canaan. Forgiven people are called to exclusive loyalty.

Finally, the radiant face of Moses was meant to show Israel what it meant to have a mediator who spoke with God. His face confirmed that the words he brought were from the LORD. The people's fear, verse 30, and Moses' call to come near, verse 31, taught them to receive God's word through God's servant.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The proclamation of God's name is not tied to its moment. It is a revelation of who God is, and Scripture treats it as true for every generation. Believers still pray it, as the psalms do, and rest on it.

The covenant terms are a different matter. The feasts, the redemption of firstborn animals, and the law about the young goat were given to Israel under the Sinai covenant. The New Testament treats the festival calendar as 'a shadow of the things to come,' whose substance 'belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:16-17. Christ is 'our Passover lamb,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and the Feast of Weeks finds its fullness in Pentecost. Christians are not bound to the calendar, but they learn from it that time, harvest and household belong to God.

The prohibition of covenants and marriages with the Canaanites was aimed at the danger of idolatry, verses 15 and 16. Its principle continues in Paul's counsel, 'Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers,' 2 Corinthians 6:14, though its ethnic application to the nations of Canaan does not.

Moses' shining face and veil are described, not commanded. They belong to his unique office, and Paul reads them as a sign of the difference between the old covenant and the new.

debates.question: How do God's forgiving love and His visiting iniquity on children and grandchildren, verse 7, fit together?

views.label: Generational consequences, not inherited guilt
views.case: Many interpreters read this as describing the observable, natural consequences of sin patterns passed down through families and communities, not a claim that God punishes individuals for sins they did not personally commit, consistent with Ezekiel 18's insistence that each person is judged for their own sin.

views.label: Covenant solidarity within a household or nation
views.case: Others see this within the ancient near eastern understanding of corporate solidarity, where a household or nation could experience shared consequences of a leader's or community's sin, while still affirming, as the text itself does, that God's loving devotion to a thousand generations vastly outweighs judgment to the third or fourth.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the text emphasizes that God's mercy vastly outweighs His judgment in scope and duration, and neither reading understands this as contradicting personal responsibility for one's own sin, as later Scripture clarifies.

debates.question: Who wrote on the second tablets, the LORD or Moses?

views.label: The LORD wrote the Ten Words; Moses wrote the other terms
views.case: God says in verse 1, 'I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets,' and Deuteronomy 10:4 confirms that 'the LORD wrote on the tablets.' On this reading verse 27 tells Moses to write down 'these words,' the covenant terms of verses 10 to 26, while the 'He' of verse 28 who wrote the Ten Commandments on the tablets is the LORD. Hebrew narrative often shifts subject without naming it.

views.label: Moses wrote at God's command
views.case: Others read verse 28 in its most natural flow, with Moses as the subject throughout: he was there forty days, he did not eat, and he wrote on the tablets. On this view God's promise to write in verse 1 is fulfilled through His servant, as much of Scripture is written by human authors at God's direction.

debates.bearing: Deuteronomy 10:4 settles the question for many readers in favour of the first view. Either way the chapter's point is that the renewed covenant carries the same words and the same authority as the first. The broken covenant is not replaced by a lesser one; it is restored in full.

debates.question: Why did Moses veil his face: to spare the people, or, as Paul says, to hide the fading glory?

views.label: The Exodus account on its own terms
views.case: In Exodus the people are afraid to approach, verse 30, and Moses wears the veil when he is not speaking God's words, removing it before the LORD and while delivering God's commands, verses 33 to 35. On this reading the veil marks off Moses' ordinary life from his role as God's spokesman, and perhaps shields the people from a glory they could not bear.

views.label: Paul's reading of the fading
views.case: Paul says Moses put a veil over his face 'to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away,' 2 Corinthians 3:13. Exodus does not say the glory faded, but the repeated removal and replacement of the veil implies that Moses needed to return to the LORD for his face to shine again. Paul draws out that implication to show that the old covenant's glory was real but temporary.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals. Exodus describes what the veil did in Moses' day, and Paul, reading the whole story in the light of Christ, explains what it signified. Paul's point is not that Moses was deceptive, but that the old covenant's glory depended on a mediator who kept having to go back, while the new covenant gives lasting access in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
The proclamation of verses 6 and 7 is dense with words that shaped the Bible's vocabulary for God, and several go beyond the two adjectives the basic text names.

'Slow to anger' is erekh appayim, literally 'long of nostrils.' The Hebrew word for anger, af, is also the word for nose, probably from the flaring of the nostrils in rage. To be long of nostrils is to take a long breath before anger kindles. The same phrase describes the patient person in Proverbs, and it is this patience that Jonah resented, Jonah 4:2.

'Abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness' translates rav chesed ve'emet. Chesed is covenant love, the loyal kindness that keeps faith with a bond freely made. Emet, from the root aman, to be firm, means reliability or truth. The pair appears often in the psalms, and many readers hear it behind John's 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14. The BSB footnote to verse 7 notes that 'to a thousand generations' reads in Hebrew simply 'to thousands,' though Deuteronomy 7:9 spells it out as 'a thousand generations.'

'Forgiving' is nose, from nasa, to lift or carry. Forgiveness in this idiom is the lifting away of guilt, and the same verb describes the scapegoat that 'will carry on itself all their iniquities,' Leviticus 16:22. The objects are the three main Hebrew words for wrongdoing: avon, iniquity or twistedness, pesha, transgression or rebellion, and chatta'ah, sin as missing the mark. Leviticus 16:21 gathers the same three on the Day of Atonement, and Psalm 32:1-2 opens with all three. God forgives every kind of wrong.

'He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished' is an emphatic construction, the infinitive set beside the finite verb of naqah, to be clean or acquitted: literally 'clearing He will not clear.' Jeremiah 30:11 and Nahum 1:3 repeat the phrase.

'Visit' is paqad, a verb that means to attend to, to inspect, or to deal with. It can be gracious, as when God 'will surely visit you' in Genesis 50:24 and 'I have surely attended to you' in Exodus 3:16. Here it is the attention of a judge. The same verb described the 'day I settle accounts' in Exodus 32:34.

In verse 14 God's name is 'Jealous,' qanna. Divine jealousy in the Old Testament is the zeal of a husband for an exclusive marriage, which is why verses 15 and 16 describe idolatry as prostitution. Paul applies the same idea when he says, 'I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy,' 2 Corinthians 11:2.

'I am making a covenant,' verse 10, is literally 'I am cutting a covenant,' karat berit, the standard idiom for making a binding agreement, perhaps recalling the cutting of animals in covenant rites, Genesis 15:10. The Ten Commandments of verse 28 are in Hebrew 'the Ten Words,' as the BSB footnote says, the same phrase as Deuteronomy 4:13 and 10:4.

Finally, 'radiant' in verses 29, 30 and 35 is qaran, related to qeren, horn, perhaps because rays of light were pictured like horns. The Septuagint rendered it with a verb meaning 'was glorified,' and that choice lies behind Paul's language of glory in 2 Corinthians 3:7.

typology.type: The second tablets laid up in the ark, Exodus 34:1 and Deuteronomy 10:1-5
typology.fulfillment: The words God wrote a second time were placed in the ark, the box beneath the mercy seat, and there they remained. The law was kept safe at the centre of Israel's worship, but not in Israel's heart. The psalmist speaks of a servant who says, 'Your law is within my heart,' Psalm 40:8, and Hebrews 10:5-7 applies that psalm to Christ. In Him the law is kept perfectly, and through Him God writes His laws on His people's hearts, Hebrews 10:16. The type falls short because stone tablets in a box could guard the law but not produce obedience; the new covenant gives both.

typology.type: Moses' face shining after speaking with the LORD, Exodus 34:29-35
typology.fulfillment: Moses' face shone with a reflected light; he 'was unaware,' verse 29, that it had happened. On the mountain of transfiguration Jesus' face 'shone like the sun,' Matthew 17:2, not by reflection but because He is 'the radiance of God's glory,' Hebrews 1:3. Paul then says believers who look to the Lord 'all reflect the glory of the Lord' and are being transformed, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The escalation runs from one mediator's borrowed shining to the source of light Himself, and then to a whole people changed by beholding Him. Moses' radiance had to be renewed by returning to the tent; the believer's transformation is ongoing by the Spirit.

typology.type: The mediator's forty days and nights without food, Exodus 34:28
typology.fulfillment: Moses stayed with the LORD forty days and forty nights, neither eating nor drinking, receiving the covenant for a people who had broken it. Jesus, after His baptism, fasted 'forty days and forty nights' in the wilderness, Matthew 4:2, and answered each temptation from Deuteronomy, the book of Moses' sermons. Where Israel had failed in the wilderness, the Son stood firm. The type falls short because Moses fasted as a sinful man pleading for sinners, Deuteronomy 9:18, while Jesus fasted as the sinless Son, preparing to bear sin Himself and to establish a covenant that cannot be broken.

typology.type: The firstborn redeemed by a lamb, Exodus 34:19-20
typology.fulfillment: Every firstborn belonged to God, and firstborn sons were to be redeemed, a standing memorial of the Passover night when Israel's firstborn were spared. Luke records that Jesus, as a firstborn son, was presented to the Lord in keeping with this law, Luke 2:22-23. Yet He is Himself the lamb by which others are redeemed: 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and believers are redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. The firstborn who was presented to God became the redemption price for all God's people.

study.christ:
The name God proclaims in verses 6 and 7 is the portrait the Gospels hold up to Jesus. John says the Word became flesh, 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, and that 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17. Whether or not John had these exact Hebrew words in mind, he presents Jesus as the embodiment of the God Moses heard proclaimed on the mountain. What was spoken in a cloud at Sinai is lived out in Galilee.

Each part of the name can be traced in Christ's ministry. He 'was moved with compassion' for the crowds, Matthew 9:36. He was patient, slow to anger, with disciples who kept failing to understand. And He did what the proclamation reserves for God: He forgave sins. When Jesus told the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven,' the scribes asked, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' Mark 2:5-7. They were right about the principle, and Jesus claims it.

The other half of the name is not set aside in Christ. God 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' verse 7. The cross is the place where that clause and the clause about forgiveness are kept together. Paul says God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26. At Sinai, forgiveness was proclaimed and guilt was visited; at Calvary, both happen in one act.

The chapter also points to Christ as the mediator of a better covenant. Moses came down from the mountain with a covenant renewed and a face shining. Hebrews contrasts the terrifying mountain of Sinai with Mount Zion, where believers come 'to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant,' Hebrews 12:18-24. Moses' face frightened the people so that they would not come near, verse 30. Jesus' glory draws sinners in.

The Feast of Weeks of verse 22 becomes a signpost to Christ's work through the Spirit. Fifty days after the Passover in which Christ was sacrificed, on the day of Pentecost, the Spirit is given, Acts 2:1. Paul says Christ Himself is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the harvest festivals of Exodus 34 become pictures of the resurrection harvest.

Care is needed not to over-read the ceremonial laws. The young goat and the donkey are not coded prophecies. The New Testament's own links are through the name, the mediator, the feasts that it explicitly connects to Christ, and Paul's reading of the veil. Those are enough to show that the God who renewed the covenant at Sinai is the God who came in Jesus.
study.god:
This chapter is the Old Testament's own definition of God. When Moses asked to see His glory, God did not show a form but spoke His name and then explained it. The God of Israel is known first by what He says He is.

He takes the initiative in restoration. Moses had broken the tablets; God tells him to cut new ones and promises to write on them again, verse 1. He 'descended in a cloud, stood with him there,' verse 5. After the calf, it would have been just for God to walk away. Instead He comes down, stands beside His servant, and passes by in grace.

His character is weighted toward mercy. Five phrases describe compassion, grace, patience, loving devotion and faithfulness before any mention of judgment. His loving devotion reaches 'to a thousand generations,' while the visitation of iniquity reaches three or four. This is not a balance of equal forces. Mercy is the larger reality, and Lamentations 3:22 can say, 'Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed.'

Yet His mercy never becomes indifference to evil. The one who forgives 'iniquity, transgression, and sin' also 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' verse 7. The two are not in contradiction. His forgiveness is costly precisely because He takes guilt seriously. Psalm 130:4 captures the effect: 'with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared.'

He is jealous, verse 14. God's jealousy is not insecurity but the proper zeal of One who is supremely worthy and who loves His people too much to share them with gods that would destroy them. His name is Jealous because His love is exclusive, like a husband's, Hosea 2:19-20.

He is the Lord of time, harvest and household. The feasts claim Israel's calendar, the firstborn claim its families and herds, and the firstfruits claim its fields, verses 18 to 26. God also guards what He claims: while every man goes up to worship, 'no one will covet your land,' verse 24.

He does wonders that reveal Him to the nations. 'All the people among whom you live will see the LORD's work, for it is an awesome thing that I am doing with you,' verse 10. God's dealings with Israel are public; they display His character to the world.

And His glory changes those who are near Him. Moses' face shone because he had been speaking with the LORD, verse 29. God's holiness is not only dangerous but transforming. For worship, the chapter offers both a model and a creed. Moses 'immediately bowed down to the ground and worshiped,' verse 8, and every generation since has worshipped by saying back to God the name He proclaimed there.

crossReferences.note: The second commandment already contained the pattern of verse 7: iniquity visited to the third and fourth generations of those who hate God, loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Him. Exodus 34 repeats the pattern after the calf but places mercy first and expands it into a full description of God's character.

When Israel refuses to enter the land, Moses quotes this proclamation back to God as the basis of his prayer, asking for pardon 'in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion.' God answers, 'I have pardoned them as you requested.' The name of Exodus 34 becomes the ground of intercession.

Jonah quotes the formula as a complaint. He fled because he knew God was 'gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion,' and would spare Nineveh. The prophet's anger shows that the mercy proclaimed at Sinai reaches beyond Israel, to the discomfort of those who want it kept for themselves.

Nahum quotes the other half of the proclamation against Nineveh: the LORD is slow to anger, but 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.' Read with Jonah, it shows that the same name holds both mercy for the repentant and judgment for the persistently guilty.

Micah turns the name of Exodus 34 into a hymn of wonder: 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?' God will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. The prophet takes the words about forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin and pictures them as a complete removal of guilt.

The psalm quotes verse 6 and then expands it. God does not deal with us according to our sins; His loving devotion is as high as the heavens; He removes transgressions as far as the east is from the west. It is a meditation on what it means for God to be slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion.

Moses' later account of the second tablets. He adds that he made an ark of acacia wood, that the LORD wrote on the tablets what had been written before, and that the tablets were placed in the ark, 'and there they have remained.' This supports reading the LORD as the writer of the Ten Words.

John describes the incarnate Word as 'full of grace and truth,' language many hear as an echo of 'loving devotion and faithfulness' in Exodus 34:6, and then sets Moses and Jesus side by side: 'the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.' The name proclaimed at Sinai takes flesh.

Jesus tells a paralysed man, 'your sins are forgiven,' and the scribes object, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' Exodus 34:7 names forgiving iniquity as God's own work. Jesus' claim to forgive is a claim to be the God who proclaimed His name to Moses.

Paul reads Moses' veil as a sign. Moses covered his face over a glory that was passing away; a veil still lies over hearts when the old covenant is read, and it is removed only in Christ. Those who turn to the Lord behold His glory unveiled and are transformed into His image.

The writer contrasts Sinai, with its fire, darkness and terror, with Mount Zion and 'Jesus the mediator of a new covenant.' The people who were afraid to approach Moses' shining face, Exodus 34:30, are answered by a congregation invited to draw near to God through Christ.

study.oneStory:
In the Bible's story, God's clearest self-revelation keeps coming after human failure. After Adam's sin came the first promise of a seed, Genesis 3:15. After the flood came the covenant with Noah. And after Israel's first great betrayal at Sinai comes the fullest description of God's character in the Old Testament. The name of Exodus 34:6-7 is spoken not to a faithful people but to a forgiven one.

That name becomes the thread by which Israel's history is held together. When Israel rebels at the edge of the land, Moses prays it, Numbers 14:18. When the nation is carried into exile and returns, the Levites confess it, Nehemiah 9:17. When prophets call for repentance, they appeal to it, Joel 2:13. When God spares a pagan city, His prophet quotes it in anger, Jonah 4:2, and the nations learn that this mercy is not for Israel alone. The whole Old Testament can be read as God proving His name true.

Yet the story also shows the limits of the Sinai covenant. The tablets were rewritten, but the people's hearts were not. Jeremiah looks back on 'a covenant they broke' and promises a new one in which God will write His law on their hearts and 'remember their sins no more,' Jeremiah 31:31-34. The veil on Moses' face becomes, in Paul's reading, a sign that the old covenant's glory could not last, 2 Corinthians 3:13.

The name finds its full expression in Christ. In Him God's compassion walks among the sick and sinful, His forgiveness is spoken to the guilty, and on the cross His refusal to clear the guilty and His forgiveness of sinners meet in one act, Romans 3:25-26. Then at Pentecost, on the Feast of Weeks named in Exodus 34:22, the Spirit is given, and the law begins to be written on hearts, Acts 2:1.

The story ends where Moses' face pointed. In the new creation God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4. The name once proclaimed to one man on a mountain is written on a whole people. There is no need for a veil, and no need for the sun, 'for the Lord God will shine on them,' Revelation 22:5. The righteous 'will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father,' Matthew 13:43, reflecting forever the glory that Moses carried down the mountain for a little while.

quiz.q: What did God command Moses to bring up the mountain to replace the broken tablets?

options.text: Two stone tablets, chiseled by Moses himself, like the originals.
options.note: Verses 1 and 4 describe Moses chiseling out these replacement tablets.

options.text: A scroll made of papyrus.
options.note: The replacement was stone tablets, not a papyrus scroll.

options.text: Nothing; the original tablets were repaired.
options.note: The original tablets were shattered beyond repair in chapter 32; entirely new tablets were required.

options.text: No replacement is mentioned.
options.note: Verses 1 and 4 explicitly describe the new stone tablets Moses chiseled out.

quiz.q: How does God describe His own character in verses 6 to 7?

options.text: Compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished.
options.note: This is the exact proclamation recorded in verses 6 to 7.

options.text: Distant and unconcerned with human affairs.
options.note: The proclamation describes God as deeply compassionate and engaged, not distant or unconcerned.

options.text: Only merciful, with no mention of justice.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly balances mercy with the statement that God will not leave the guilty unpunished.

options.text: No description of God's character is given.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 explicitly proclaim God's name and character in detail.

quiz.q: What specific danger did God warn Israel about regarding the nations in the land?

options.text: Making treaties and intermarrying with them, leading to idolatry.
options.note: Verses 12 to 16 describe this exact danger in detail.

options.text: Losing military battles against them.
options.note: The warning centers on spiritual compromise through treaties and intermarriage, not military defeat.

options.text: Adopting their system of weights and measures.
options.note: No such economic warning is given; the danger concerns idolatrous worship through alliance and intermarriage.

options.text: No warning is given about the nations.
options.note: Verses 12 through 16 explicitly warn against treaties and intermarriage leading to idolatry.

quiz.q: How long did Moses remain on the mountain this time, according to verse 28?

options.text: Forty days and forty nights, without eating bread or drinking water.
options.note: Verse 28 states this exact duration and fasting.

options.text: Seven days only.
options.note: Seven days describes the ordination period in chapter 29; this stay on Sinai lasted forty days and nights.

options.text: A single day and night.
options.note: The stay was far longer, forty days and nights, matching his earlier time on the mountain in chapter 24.

options.text: No duration is specified.
options.note: Verse 28 explicitly states forty days and forty nights.

quiz.q: Why did Moses begin wearing a veil over his face?

options.text: Because his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD, and the Israelites were afraid to approach him.
options.note: Verses 29 to 33 describe both the radiance and the people's fear that led to the veil.

options.text: To hide a physical injury sustained on the mountain.
options.note: The text describes radiant glory from God's presence, not any injury, as the reason for the veil.

options.text: As a sign of mourning for the golden calf.
options.note: The veil specifically addressed his radiant face and the people's fear, not an act of mourning.

options.text: No reason is given for the veil.
options.note: Verses 29 through 33 explicitly explain the radiance and resulting need for a veil.

questions: God's proclaimed name holds together compassion and justice without contradiction. Which of these two truths about God do you find easier to believe, and which do you tend to neglect?
Moses immediately bowed down and worshiped after hearing God's name proclaimed. What would it look like for a fuller understanding of who God is to move you to worship rather than mere information?

The covenant renewal warned against gradual compromise through alliances and intermarriage with idolatrous nations. Where in your own life are small, ongoing compromises quietly pulling you away from wholehearted devotion to God?
Moses' face was radiant, yet he himself was unaware of it. Where have you seen evidence of God's work in your own life that others noticed before you did?

Moses' glory faded and needed to be veiled again and again, but believers now behold Christ's unfading glory with unveiled faces. How does knowing your access to God's glory in Christ never needs to be veiled change how boldly you approach Him?

translationNotes.note: This proclamation of God's name becomes the most frequently echoed description of God's character throughout the rest of the Old Testament, quoted or alluded to in Numbers 14:18, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, and Nehemiah 9:17.

Visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren likely describes observable generational consequences of sin rather than inherited guilt for another's sin, a point later clarified explicitly in Ezekiel 18:20.

His face had become radiant translates a Hebrew phrase related to the word for horn, qaran, which some ancient interpreters, including in certain classical artistic traditions, misunderstood as horns rather than rays of light; the context of radiance from God's presence makes clear that light, not horns, is intended.
